newsitem.title: USA: Backers of hamburger futures bullish on prospects.
newsitem.headline: Backers of hamburger futures bullish on prospects.

text.p: Chicago's free-wheeling futures traders are waiting eagerly to sink their teeth into what promises to be a tasty new commodity that debuts on Monday -- hamburger futures.
The futures contracts -- with each one representing 20,000 pounds of boneless ground beef -- have many livestock analysts and meat traders convinced they have a successful new market.
"I think it's got a bright future," said Andy Gottschalk, livestock analyst with Linnco Futures Group in Englewood, Colorado.
Gottschalk predicted an active use of the contracts from anyone in the ground beef business seeking price protection.

That group includes cattle ranchers, beef packers and meat processors, supermarket chains and retail stores, and restaurants, said Tim Brennan, a governor at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange which is listing the new contracts.
"This is a tremendous market," said Brennan. "Over 50 percent of beef consumed in this country is ground beef.
"We consume over nine billion pounds of ground beef per year, and over eight billion pounds is produced in the U.S. with the rest imported," Brennan said.
The CME already operates successful futures markets in live and feeder cattle and pork belly and lean hog contracts. It also lists butter and milk futures and trades cash cheese.

The appeal of futures -- which shadow cash prices and so allow commercial firms to "hedge" or take insuring, opposite positions in commodities to offset price risk -- always rises when cash markets can be volatile, as in beef.

Traders say even though commercial hamburger users could use the live cattle contract to hedge, cash prices of hamburger sometimes move differently than those of live cattle and the hamburger contract will let them hedge more effectively.
"This stuff is going to have some volatility," said Jack Weaver, a livestock analyst with Refco Inc in Chicago. "Prices can move rapidly, a five or 10-cent move is not unusual.
"This is not a one-cent-move market," Weaver said.

Volatility also attracts speculators, especially the "locals" who provide the trading volumes that can make or break a futures contract. The CME will allow speculators from its huge financial futures pits to freely trade the bonelss beef contract in order to maximize trading by locals.
Seasonal demand factors and cyclical cattle production trends should add to the volatile price swings in boneless beef prices, livestock analysts and beef traders said.
There will be two new contracts, one for boneless beef which is 90 percent lean (BB) and one for boneless beef trimmings which are 50 percent lean (TR).
The two contracts have been designed in partnership with the ground beef industry, which uses both 90 percent and 50 percent lean or "fat-free" material for blending purposes.

The two are blended, as well as various leans in between, to produce the 73 to 82 percent lean ground beef preferred by fast-food giants like McDonalds and Wendy's and the 80 to 85 percent leans that are mainstays at retail grocery stores, according to a study by Ohio consultant Pennington and Co.
The contract size of 20,000 pounds will allow companies who use partial loads or who either buy or produce blended to use the contracts to hedge, exchange documents said.

Each contract will be quoted in cents per pound, with a miminum price increment of $0.001 or $20 per tick. Daily price limits will be $0.03 per pound (or $600 per contract) with no limits on price moves during a contract's last 5 trading days.
The contracts will not call for actual delivery of beef.

Instead, delivery will be settled in cash payments based on CME weighted average prices for 90 percent boneless beef or 50 percent lean trimmings as calculated from daily Agriculture Department Market News reports.
Listed months for the contracts will be February, April, June, August, October and December, as in live cattle futures.

The two new contracts will be launched on Monday, June 16, at 1000 CDT, with options on the futures eligible for trading on Tuesday. Regular trading times for futures and options will be 0850-1300 CDT, starting on Tuesday.
